terms.grammar: coquō, coquere, coxī, coctum, with cēnam; of lunch, prandium coquere
evidence: Plaut. Aul. 458: ī et cēnam coque
Plaut. Ps. 890: intrō abī et cēnam coque
terms.comment: What Plautus’s masters say to the hired cook. The same verb serves for lunch, prandium coquere or percoquere. For a breakfast that is set out rather than cooked, jentāculum parāre (see the next term).

evidence: Phaedr. 3.19.2: parāre cēnam jussus est mātūrius
terms.comment: The wider phrase: getting the meal ready, cooking and all, as Aesop is told to do. See “prepare”.

phrases.latin: Tū holera lavā; ego cēnam coquam.
phrases.english: You wash the vegetables; I’ll make dinner.

phrases.latin: intrō abī et cēnam coque. properā.
phrases.english: Go inside and cook the dinner. Hurry.

phrases.latin: Jubē domī mī tibique tuaeque uxōrī celeriter cēnam coquī.
phrases.english: Have dinner cooked at home for me, for you, and for your wife, and quickly.

phrases.latin: Aesōpus dominō sōlus cum esset familia, parāre cēnam jussus est mātūrius.
phrases.english: Aesop, the only slave his master had, was told to get dinner ready earlier than usual.

sources: Lewis & Short: coquo · Lewis & Short: percoquo · Lewis & Short: cena · Lewis & Short: prandium · Lewis & Short: paro
